q: Backtracking explores the state space tree in which order?
explain: It extends one partial solution as far as possible and goes back only when stuck. Branch and bound (topics 31–32) uses breadth-first or least-cost order.

q: What is the bounding function in backtracking?
options: A test that kills a partial solution which cannot lead to a valid answer
A limit on the recursion depth
The cost of the best solution so far
A function that sorts the choices
explain: If the test fails, the whole subtree below that node is skipped. For N-Queens the test is 'the new queen is not attacked'.

q: Queens are at (row, column) = (1, 2) and (2, 4). Can a third queen go at (3, 1)?
options: No, same column as a queen
explain: Column 1 is free. |1 − 2| = 1 ≠ 3 − 1 = 2 and |1 − 4| = 3 ≠ 3 − 2 = 1, so no diagonal clash. This is the partial solution (2, 4, 1) that leads to (2, 4, 1, 3).

q: How many solutions does the 4-Queens problem have?
How many solutions does the 8-Queens problem have?
explain: 92 in total. Grouping rotations and reflections together leaves 12 essentially different ones.

q: Two queens at (r1, c1) and (r2, c2) are on the same diagonal exactly when…
explain: Moving along a diagonal changes the row and the column by the same amount.

q: Backtracking always runs in polynomial time because it prunes the tree.
explain: False. Pruning helps a lot in practice, but the worst case is still exponential.

q: What must the code do right after the recursive call returns?
options: Undo the choice that was made before the call
explain: Removing the queen (and its column and diagonals) restores the state so the next choice starts from a correct board.

q: In the Python code, all squares on one '\' diagonal share which value?
explain: Moving down-right adds 1 to both r and c, so r − c stays the same. The '/' diagonals share r + c.

q: Which problem is NOT usually solved by backtracking?
options: Single-source shortest paths with non-negative weights
explain: Dijkstra solves shortest paths in polynomial time. The other three are NP-hard search problems where backtracking is the standard exact method.
